title: Think-Aloud Modeling
preview: Say every thought in your head as you solve a problem. Students hear how an expert thinks, not just what the expert does.

body.summary: Think-Aloud Modeling means you talk out loud while you solve a problem — even the parts that feel obvious. Students don't get to see inside your head. When you say "Okay, I see two numbers and the word 'each' — that means I need to multiply," you're showing them how to think, not just what the answer is. You do not need to be a math expert to do this. You just need to narrate every single step you take, including the moments you pause, reread, or double-check.
body.whenToUse:
Use this when a student is stuck and doesn't know where to start, or when you're introducing a new kind of problem. It's especially powerful right before you ask students to try one themselves. You want them to hear the thinking before they have to do the thinking.

Avoid rushing. If the think-aloud feels too fast, it probably is. Real thinking includes pauses.
body.howToImplement:
1. PICK ONE PROBLEM to model. Not two, not three. One. Keep it short.

2. BEFORE YOU START, say: "I'm going to show you what's in my head while I solve this. When I stop to think, you'll hear me say it out loud."

3. NARRATE EVERY STEP. Here's what that sounds like:
   • "First, I'm reading the whole problem."
   • "I see the word 'each' — I'm going to underline it because that word usually tells me to multiply."
   • "The two numbers are 6 and 4. Let me write 6 × 4 on my paper."
   • "Wait — let me reread the question to make sure I'm answering what it asks."
   • "Okay, 6 × 4 = 24. I'm going to write the answer with a label so I remember what it means."

4. INCLUDE MISTAKES. Pretend to start the wrong way, then catch yourself: "Oh — I almost added. But the word 'each' means multiply. Let me fix that." This is one of the most powerful moves.

5. AFTER YOU FINISH, ask: "What did you hear me do before I wrote anything down?" (Answer: read, underline, think.)
body.teacherMoves:
IF you feel awkward talking to yourself:
→ That's normal. Say: "I'm going to be a little silly and talk out loud so you can hear my brain working." Students find it charming.

IF a student interrupts with an answer:
→ Say: "Hold that thought — I'm still thinking out loud. You'll get a turn to try one next."

IF you don't know the math yourself:
→ That's okay. Read the answer key provided in this packet. Then walk through the steps out loud as if you are figuring it out, pausing at each step: "The answer shows 24. Let me see how that works... 6 × 4... yes, that's 24."

IF a student says "I don't get it" after your think-aloud:
→ Ask: "What's the first thing you heard me do?" Start there. They usually know more than they think.

IF you're running short on time:
→ Focus the think-aloud on just the FIRST STEP. "Watch me decide what to do first." That's often where students are stuck.
body.variations:
TIER 2 (Scaffolded):
Use as described. Write each step on the board as you say it so students can see AND hear your thinking.

TIER 3 (Heavily Scaffolded):
Do a mini think-aloud on a simpler version of the problem first. For example, if the real problem uses 84 ÷ 7, do your think-aloud on 10 ÷ 2. Same structure, smaller numbers. Then tell them: "Now watch me do the same thing with bigger numbers."

PARTNER THINK-ALOUD:
After you model, have students pair up. One student solves while talking out loud, the other listens. Then they swap. This makes the thinking visible for the partner AND forces the solver to slow down.
body.researchBase: Think-Alouds are rooted in Vygotsky's work on making expert thinking visible, and they're one of the most evidence-backed instructional moves in math and literacy intervention (Bauman, Jones, & Seifert-Kessell, 1993). The What Works Clearinghouse lists explicit modeling as one of the top-rated practices for Tier 2 and Tier 3 math intervention (Gersten et al., 2009).
body.inlineTip: Before anyone writes, solve this problem out loud yourself. Narrate EVERY step — including pausing, rereading, and catching yourself.
